questions.text: Every change that passes the required checks on main goes to production automatically, with no human approval. Which practice is this?
options: Continuous integration
Continuous delivery
Continuous deployment
Trunk-based branching
questions.explanation: Continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically. Continuous delivery also produces a deployable artifact for every passing change, but production deployment can wait for an explicit decision or approval.

questions.text: A team's pipeline builds a deployable image for every merge, deploys it to staging, and waits for a release manager to approve production. Which practice does this describe?
options: Continuous delivery
Continuous deployment
Blue/green deployment
Feature flagging
questions.explanation: In continuous delivery, a passing change produces a deployable artifact, and the production deployment can require an explicit approval. Continuous deployment would release it automatically.

questions.text: Staging tested an image built from commit a1b2c3. The production job rebuilds a new image from the same commit and deploys it. What is the main problem?
options: Production deployments must always use the latest tag
The rebuilt image may differ from the one that was tested
Rebuilding is fine as long as the source commit matches
Production must be built from a separate release branch
questions.explanation: Rebuilds can pick up different dependencies, base images or build tools. Build once, record the artifact digest and promote that same artifact between environments, keeping environment configuration separate.

questions.text: A release record says only myapp:latest. Why is this insufficient for reproducing what was deployed?
options: The latest tag cannot be pulled by Kubernetes nodes
Registries delete images tagged latest after a week
A tag can be moved, so it does not identify fixed content
The latest tag always points to the oldest image pushed
questions.explanation: Tags are mutable and can be reassigned to new images. Record the source revision and the immutable artifact digest so the release can be identified and reproduced exactly.

questions.text: A deployment job is triggered both by the merged pull request event and by the resulting push to main. Each merge deploys twice. What should the team do?
options: Add a retry so the second deployment overwrites the first
Run the deployment job in a larger runner to finish first
Choose one event to own deployment and document that choice
Trigger deployments from every pull request event instead
questions.explanation: Opening and merging a pull request are separate events, and a merge also creates a push. Decide which event owns each step so the same release is not deployed twice, and serialize conflicting deployments.

questions.text: During a rolling update, what must the team plan for?
options: Old and new versions serving traffic at the same time
Running two full production environments in parallel
Exposing the change only to staff before any customer
Taking the service fully offline between the batches
questions.explanation: A rolling update replaces instances in batches, so old and new versions coexist until it finishes. Both must handle the same data, messages and API contracts. A second full environment describes blue/green.

questions.text: A team wants to switch all traffic between two complete environments in one step and switch back quickly if needed. Which strategy fits, and what is its main cost?
options: Canary, with the cost of a long and careful observation window
Blue/green, needing extra capacity and data compatibility
Rolling update, with old and new instances coexisting
Feature flags, needing a flag service for every user
questions.explanation: Blue/green prepares a second environment and switches traffic to it. It needs extra capacity, and both environments usually share data, so the schema must suit both versions.

questions.text: What is the difference between a feature flag and a traffic-based canary?
options: A flag routes requests between versions; a canary toggles code paths
A flag toggles behavior inside code; a canary picks a version per request
A flag needs a second full environment; a canary needs no monitoring at all
A flag is used only in staging; a canary is used only in production
questions.explanation: A feature flag controls behavior inside already-deployed code, while a traffic-based canary controls which version handles requests. They can be combined, and both separate deploying code from exposing it.

questions.text: Version 2 ran a migration that dropped a column version 1 reads. Rolling back to version 1 makes every request fail. What was the underlying mistake?
options: The old artifact had been deleted from the registry
The rollback should have used a canary at 1% first
The migration was not backward compatible with version 1
The team should have restored the database to last week
questions.explanation: Application rollback works only if the older version can still read the current data and configuration. Backward-compatible (expand-and-contract) migrations keep the previous release usable; restoring the database would discard later writes.

questions.text: A CI job's dependency cache is evicted, and the next run is slower but produces the same test results. How should this be viewed?
options: Correct behavior: a cache should affect only speed, not results
A release failure, because the cache is the deployable artifact
A security incident, because caches hold production secrets
A flaky test, which should be rerun until the cache is restored
questions.explanation: Caches are speed optimizations; a miss should change timing, not correctness. The build artifact is what gets published and promoted, so keep caches and release artifacts distinct.

questions.text: A test fails about one run in ten, and developers rerun the pipeline until it passes. What is the better response?
options: Mark the test as optional so merges are never blocked
Add an automatic retry that reruns the job three times
Investigate it and give the flaky test a visible owner
Increase the pipeline timeout so the test has more time
questions.explanation: Rerunning until green hides the cause and erodes trust in CI. Investigate recurring failures, make the flaky test's owner and repair plan visible, and fix its dependence on timing, order or shared state.

questions.text: Which ordering of CI checks gives the fastest useful feedback?
options: Full end-to-end suite first, then unit tests if time permits
Lint and unit tests first, then integration, then focused E2E
Integration tests first, then formatting checks before merge
Manual QA first, then unit tests on the release branch only
questions.explanation: Start with fast checks such as formatting, linting, static analysis and unit tests, add integration tests for important boundaries, and keep slower end-to-end tests focused on essential user journeys.

questions.text: A project has 95% line coverage, yet a bug in an error-handling path reached production. What does this illustrate?
options: Coverage should be raised to 100% to prevent such bugs
Coverage shows code ran, not that tests catch failures
Error-handling paths cannot be tested by unit tests
Coverage tools ignore code that throws exceptions
questions.explanation: A coverage percentage reveals untested code but not whether tests assert meaningful behavior. Test important behavior and failure paths; review any threshold as the code changes.

questions.text: Two pull requests each pass CI on their own. After both merge, main fails its tests. What should the team do?
options: Nothing, because each change was verified separately
Disable the failing test until the next planned release cycle
Repair or revert the change quickly so main stays usable
Move all future work onto long-lived feature branches
questions.explanation: Individually passing changes can interact badly, so CI also verifies the integrated main branch. When main breaks, repair or revert promptly so other work can continue.

questions.text: A required check was skipped because of a path filter, and the pull request shows no test results. What does that mean for the change?
options: The tests passed, because skipped checks count as success
There is no evidence the tests passed for this change
The tests failed, so the pull request must be closed
The check ran on the default branch instead of the PR
questions.explanation: A check that did not run is not evidence that a test passed. Make sure required checks still report a result, for example when superseded runs are cancelled or paths are filtered.

questions.text: Integration tests pass locally but fail in CI when run in a different order, because they share rows in a database. What is the right fix?
options: Run the tests in CI in the same order as on laptops
Make each test set up and clean up its own data
Point the CI tests at the production database instead
Retry the failing tests until the order works out
questions.explanation: Tests should set up their own data and avoid relying on execution order, production services or another developer's machine. Independent tests can also be parallelized safely.

questions.text:
In this workflow, the test job cannot find the dist/ directory created by build. What fixes it?

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-sha>
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ls dist/
options: Add needs: build, since jobs then share the same runner workspace
Upload dist/ as an artifact, then add needs: build and download it
Rename the jobs so test sorts after build and runs second in order
Set timeout-minutes on build so it finishes before test
questions.explanation: Jobs run independently on separate runners unless needs declares a dependency, and they do not share a filesystem. Pass files with artifacts or other explicit storage. Steps within one job share that job's runner.

questions.text: A workflow sets permissions: contents: read at the top level. What effect does this have?
options: It blocks the workflow from checking out the repository
It limits the job token to reading repository contents
It grants read access to every secret in the organization
It makes the workflow run only on read-only branches
questions.explanation: permissions sets what the automatically provided GITHUB_TOKEN may do. Granting only contents: read follows least privilege; jobs that need more should request it explicitly.

questions.text:
Why is this step risky in a workflow triggered by pull requests?

- run: echo "Testing ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
options: Echo commands are not allowed in GitHub-hosted runners
Pull request titles are always empty in pull_request events
The untrusted title is inserted into the script before it runs
Expressions inside run are evaluated only after the step ends
questions.explanation: The expression is expanded into the shell script text, so a crafted title can inject commands. Pass external values through an env: variable and quote that variable in the script instead.

questions.text: A pull_request_target workflow checks out the pull request's head commit and runs npm test. Why is this dangerous?
options: pull_request_target cannot run tests on hosted runners
Untrusted code runs with the base repository's privileges
The workflow tests the base branch, so the PR is untested
It runs tests twice, once for each branch in the pull request
questions.explanation: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository and can access secrets and a write-capable token. Executing the contributor's code there, including install and test scripts, lets that code use those privileges.

questions.text: Why should third-party actions be referenced by a full commit SHA rather than a tag like @v6?
options: SHAs make the action run faster on hosted runners
A tag can be moved to different code; a SHA cannot
Tags are only supported for actions owned by GitHub
SHAs automatically receive security updates from GitHub
questions.explanation: Tags are mutable, so a compromised or changed tag can point to new code. Pin to a reviewed full commit SHA and update pins deliberately; the SHA does not update itself.

questions.text: A deployment job uses OIDC and requests id-token: write. What decides which cloud resources the job can access?
options: The id-token: write permission alone grants admin access
The repository's branch protection rules on main
The cloud role's trust policy and its attached permissions
The runner's operating system and installed CLI version
questions.explanation: id-token: write only allows the job to request an identity token. The cloud provider's trust policy decides which workflows may assume the role, and the role's permissions decide what it can do. Keep both narrow.

questions.text: A public repository uses a persistent self-hosted runner for pull request tests. What is the main risk?
options: Self-hosted runners cannot run Node.js test suites
PR code can access the runner and anything it can reach
Jobs on self-hosted runners ignore the permissions key
Self-hosted runners always expose the repository publicly
questions.explanation: Code run by a job can access the runner machine and its reachable resources, and a persistent runner can be tampered with for later jobs. Isolate runners used for untrusted work and replace them after use.

questions.text: A canary at 5% passed CI, but its HTTP 5xx rate is 3% against 0.2% for the stable baseline. CPU and memory look normal. What should happen?
options: Continue to 25%, because resource usage is within limits
Wait for 100% rollout to get a statistically larger sample
Stop expansion and return traffic to the stable version
Restart the canary pods so the errors clear from the logs
questions.explanation: The canary breaches an agreed error-rate stopping rule compared with the baseline, which matters more than healthy resource metrics. Stop expanding, shift traffic back to stable (with enough capacity ready) and investigate.

questions.text: A canary is shown only to internal staff for two hours and looks healthy. Why might that not justify a full rollout?
options: Staff traffic may not represent real customers' behavior
Internal users can never trigger application errors
Two hours is longer than any canary should normally run
Canaries must always start at exactly 1% of all traffic
questions.explanation: Cohort differences matter: staff or one region may use different features, devices or data than other users. Compare representative traffic, or add other evidence before expanding.

questions.text: A service receives only a few requests per hour. How should its canary be adapted?
options: Skip the canary and deploy straight to 100% at night
Use the same 10-minute window as high-traffic services
Use a longer observation window or add synthetic checks
Judge it only by CPU usage, since errors are too rare
questions.explanation: Low-volume services produce too few requests in a short window to reveal problems. Lengthen the observation window or add synthetic checks so the comparison has enough evidence.

questions.text: A release changes how a nightly batch job deletes expired records. Why does a 1% request-based canary give little protection here?
options: Batch jobs cannot be deployed with the same artifact
Background jobs can bypass the traffic split entirely
Canaries only work for read-only database queries
Deletions are always reversible with a rollback
questions.explanation: A traffic-based canary limits exposure for requests routed through the split. Background jobs and destructive data changes can affect all data regardless of the cohort, so they need separate safeguards.

questions.text: A team keeps its kubectl apply deploy script in Git and runs it from CI after each merge. Why is this not GitOps by itself?
options: GitOps forbids storing deployment logic in version control
No agent continuously reconciles the cluster with Git
GitOps requires every deployment to be approved manually
The script must be written in YAML instead of shell
questions.explanation: GitOps requires declarative desired state that agents pull and continuously reconcile. A pipeline that runs a versioned script once gives the script history but does not detect or correct later drift.

questions.text: During an incident, an engineer scales a Deployment by hand. Minutes later, Argo CD sets it back to the old replica count. What should the team do?
options: Disable the controller permanently so manual fixes persist
Delete the Deployment and recreate it with kubectl create
Record the emergency change in Git so the source matches it
Restart the controller so it forgets the previous state
questions.explanation: The controller reconciles drift according to its policy, so an undeclared manual change can be undone. Document how emergency changes are made and captured in the source of truth so reconciliation does not reverse them unexpectedly.

questions.text: A bad release deleted customer records. The team reverts the GitOps configuration commit, and the controller redeploys the previous version. What is still true?
options: The deleted records are restored along with the old version
The database schema is rolled back to match the old commit
The deleted data must be recovered through the backup plan
The revert must be repeated until the records reappear
questions.explanation: Reverting configuration can restore an earlier artifact or setting, but it does not undo database writes or restore deleted data. Verify health after reconciliation and use the recovery plan for data loss.

questions.text: A pipeline shows a green CI job for a commit. What does that tell you?
options: The commit is deployed and every user journey works
The job's configured commands finished successfully
The artifact was promoted to production automatically
The cloud account has the permissions it needs to run
questions.explanation: A green job means only that its configured commands succeeded. Read the pipeline definition to learn what it actually checked; it does not imply deployment or full functional coverage.

questions.text: A Python service using an SDK gets AccessDenied when reading an object storage bucket, even though its credentials are valid. What is the likely issue?
options: The service failed authentication and has no identity
The identity is authenticated but lacks permission
The SDK cannot read buckets without the web console
The bucket must be in the same region as the developer
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides what it may do. A valid identity can still lack access due to its policies, the bucket's policy or other restrictions.

questions.text: Before running a deployment command from your laptop, which AWS CLI command confirms which account and role your configured profile is using?
options: aws configure list-profiles
aws s3 ls --profile learning
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam list-users
questions.explanation: aws sts get-caller-identity returns the account, ARN and user or role ID for the current credentials. Check account, region and identity before making changes, and avoid sharing the output from private environments.

questions.text: A front-end team wants browser code to upload files straight to cloud storage. What is the appropriate design?
options: Embed a long-lived cloud access key in the JavaScript bundle
Have the server issue a signed URL with limited scope and expiry
Create one IAM user per website customer for direct uploads
Make the bucket publicly writable so uploads need no identity at all
questions.explanation: Browser code must not contain a server's cloud credentials, and website customers normally have application identities, not IAM users. Signed URLs allow direct access with explicit authorization and expiry.

questions.text: A CloudFormation update changes a property on a database resource. Why review the change set before executing it?
options: Change sets are only required when resources move to a new region
Executing a change set without review deletes the stack's tags
Some property changes replace the resource instead of updating it
CloudFormation never updates resources in place after creation
questions.explanation: Depending on the property, an update can modify a resource in place or replace it, and removed resources can be deleted unless retention policies apply. Review the change set and protect persistent data before executing.

questions.text: A web service works with curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/ on the server, but other machines cannot connect. ss -lnt shows the listener as 127.0.0.1:8080. What is the most likely cause?
options: The service is bound only to the loopback interface
The service is accepting UDP rather than TCP connections
The DNS record for the server has an expired TTL
The kernel has run out of ephemeral client ports
questions.explanation: A listener on 127.0.0.1 accepts connections only from the same host or network namespace. It must listen on a reachable interface (or 0.0.0.0) before firewalls or DNS even matter. ss -lnt lists TCP listeners, so UDP is not the issue.

questions.text: curl fails instantly with "Connection refused" when connecting to a server's port 9000. What does this most often indicate?
options: A firewall is silently dropping the client's packets
Nothing is listening there, or the host rejected it
The TLS certificate for the server has expired
The HTTP application returned a 5xx response
questions.explanation: A refusal is an active answer, usually because no process listens on that address and port or something explicitly rejects the connection. Silent filtering typically produces a timeout instead, and TLS or HTTP errors only appear after a connection succeeds.

questions.text: ping api.internal succeeds, but an HTTPS request to the same host times out. What can you conclude?
options: The HTTPS service must be healthy, so the client is misconfigured
The DNS answer is stale and points the client at the wrong host
The host answers ICMP, which says nothing about the TCP port or app
The TLS certificate chain is invalid and the handshake was dropped
questions.explanation: A successful ping proves only that ICMP echo works. The TCP port may be filtered, unbound or served by a stalled application. Test the actual port and protocol, for example with curl --verbose --max-time 5.

questions.text: curl --verbose https://shop.example/ prints "Could not resolve host". Which layer failed?
options: Name resolution, so no connection or TLS was attempted
TLS negotiation, after the TCP connection was established
The HTTP application, which rejected the request headers
Routing, after the client chose the server's IP address
questions.explanation: Requests are troubleshot in layers: name resolution, routing, connection, TLS, then HTTP. If the name cannot be resolved, the client never obtains an address, so the later layers never run.

questions.text: An application container calls http://localhost:5432 to reach a database running in a different container, and the connection fails. Why?
options: Containers cannot open TCP connections to databases
localhost refers to the app container's own namespace
Port 5432 is reserved for the container runtime itself
The database requires a Unix socket for every client
questions.explanation: Each container normally has its own network namespace, so localhost is the container itself, not the host or a sibling container. Use the other service's reachable name or address, such as a Compose service name.

questions.text: In the web server lab, Apache is stopped while Nginx keeps running as the reverse proxy. Which result is expected for a request to /apache/?
options: 404 Not Found, because the Apache page was removed
200 OK, because Nginx's /healthz still passes
502 Bad Gateway, because the upstream is unreachable
401 Unauthorized, because the proxy lost its session
questions.explanation: A gateway that cannot get a valid response from its upstream typically returns 502. Nginx's own /healthz checks only Nginx, so the gateway can look healthy while a dependency is down.

questions.text: A dashboard shows a jump in 5xx responses at the load balancer. What is the best first interpretation?
options: Clients are sending malformed requests or invalid credentials
A server-side component in the serving path is failing
Browsers are refusing the site's TLS certificate
DNS resolvers are returning the wrong record for the site
questions.explanation: 5xx codes indicate a server-side failure somewhere along the serving path, while 4xx usually describes a client-side request or access problem. Next, find which component generated the response: proxy, application or dependency.

questions.text: Which transport does HTTP/3 use?
options: TCP with TLS 1.2
QUIC over UDP
SCTP over IP
Raw IP datagrams
questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly run over TCP, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which runs over UDP and builds its own reliability and encryption on top.

questions.text: A sensor sends readings over UDP. The receiver sees some readings missing and others out of order. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The network is faulty, because UDP retransmits lost datagrams
The receiver is misconfigured, since UDP preserves send order
This is allowed; UDP has no delivery or ordering guarantees
The sender must switch to HTTP/2 to keep using UDP datagrams
questions.explanation: UDP provides datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. Applications that need them must add sequence numbers, acknowledgments or retries, or use a transport such as TCP.

questions.text: After changing a DNS A record to a new server, some clients keep connecting to the old address for a while. What best explains this?
options: The old server is forwarding all traffic back to itself
Resolvers cache the previous answer until its TTL expires
A records only change after the TLS certificate is renewed
Clients always pin the first IP they ever resolved for a name
questions.explanation: DNS answers are cached according to their time-to-live and resolver behavior, so clients may keep the old address until cached entries expire. Lowering the TTL ahead of a planned change shortens this window.

questions.text: A site uses HTTPS with a valid certificate. A logged-in user changes /invoices/1001 to /invoices/1002 and sees another customer's invoice. What is missing?
options: A stronger TLS cipher suite on the load balancer
A longer certificate chain from a public authority
An application authorization check on each record
A shorter DNS TTL for the application's hostname
questions.explanation: TLS authenticates the server and protects data in transit; it does not decide whether an authenticated user may access a particular record. The application must check that the invoice belongs to the requesting user.

questions.text: A browser rejects https://api.example.com with a name mismatch error. The certificate is valid and unexpired but issued only for www.example.com. What is the fix?
options: Lower the DNS TTL so browsers refetch the certificate
Serve a certificate that covers api.example.com
Switch the API to HTTP/3 so the check is skipped
Tell users to disable certificate verification
questions.explanation: TLS validation checks the chain, expiry and expected hostname. A certificate for a different name fails the hostname check, so the server needs a certificate whose names include the requested host. Disabling verification removes the protection.

questions.text: After enabling a CDN, some users see another user's account page. What is the most likely cause?
options: The CDN's TLS certificate expired during the rollout
The origin returned 5xx responses that the CDN retried
A personalized response was cached under a shared key
The DNS TTL was too short for the CDN's edge locations
questions.explanation: Cache keys and expiry affect correctness as well as performance. If a personalized response is cached under a key shared by many users, the CDN serves it to the wrong people. Mark such responses uncacheable or vary the key appropriately.

questions.text: A client's POST /payments request times out and the client wants to retry automatically. What makes the retry safe?
options: An idempotency key that the server uses to deduplicate the request
An unlimited number of immediate retries until a response arrives
Switching the request from POST to a cached GET on the retry
A longer DNS TTL so the retry reaches the same backend server
questions.explanation: The first attempt may have succeeded before the timeout, so retrying a state-changing request can charge twice. An idempotency key with server-side deduplication makes repeats harmless; retries should also be limited and use backoff.

questions.text: On a systemd-based Linux host, which command shows the logs of the nginx service?
options: du -sh /var/log/nginx
journalctl -u nginx
ps -ef | grep nginx
id nginx
questions.explanation: journalctl -u <unit> reads the systemd journal for one unit, and systemctl manages and inspects the unit itself. du shows disk usage, ps lists processes and id shows a user's identity and groups.

questions.text: You edited a file and ran git add on it. Now git diff prints nothing. How do you review what will be committed?
options: Run git log --oneline -5
Run git diff --cached
Run git status --ignored
Run git revert HEAD
questions.explanation: git diff compares the working tree with the staging area, so staged changes no longer appear there. git diff --cached shows staged changes compared with the last commit.

questions.text: A commit that broke production has already been pushed to the shared main branch, and teammates have pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1 followed by a force push
git revert <commit> and push the new commit
git commit --amend and push the amended commit
Delete main on the remote and push a fresh copy
questions.explanation: git revert records a new inverse commit, so history stays intact for everyone who has already pulled. Resetting, amending or recreating the branch rewrites shared history and disrupts other clones.

questions.text: A developer committed .env containing a database password, then deleted the file and added .env to .gitignore. What must happen next?
options: Nothing, because .gitignore removes the file from history
Only rename the variable so the old password is not used
Revoke or replace the password, since it remains in history
Make the repository private, which invalidates the secret
questions.explanation: A .gitignore rule only stops untracked files from being added; earlier commits still contain the password, and clones may already have it. Treat it as exposed: revoke or rotate it first, then plan any history cleanup.

questions.text:
A script uses set -e, but it continues after curl fails in the line below. Why?

set -e
curl -fsS https://example.com/data.json | tee data.json
echo "done"
options: set -e only applies to commands inside functions
A pipeline's status comes from tee unless pipefail is set
curl -f stops curl from ever returning a non-zero exit code
tee restarts curl automatically when it exits early
questions.explanation: Without set -o pipefail, a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command, here tee, which succeeded. With pipefail, the pipeline fails if any command in it fails, so set -e stops the script.

questions.text:
The script below is run with no arguments. Where does it write its report?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
report_dir=${1:-./reports}
mkdir -p -- "$report_dir"
df -h -- "$report_dir" > "$report_dir/disk.txt"
options: It exits with an unbound variable error from set -u
./reports/disk.txt
./disk.txt in the current directory
It prints to the terminal and writes no file
questions.explanation: ${1:-./reports} uses ./reports when the first argument is unset or empty, and this form is safe under set -u. mkdir -p creates the directory if needed, so the report lands in ./reports/disk.txt.

questions.text: Why does a rerunnable script use mkdir -p -- "$dir" instead of mkdir $dir?
options: It succeeds if the directory exists and handles spaces in the name
It deletes and recreates the directory to guarantee a clean state
It runs the command with root privileges when permission is denied
It makes the directory private to the current user automatically
questions.explanation: -p creates parent directories and does not fail when the directory already exists, so the script can run again. Quoting prevents word splitting and globbing of the value, and -- stops a name starting with - being read as an option.

questions.text: A Bash script that started as five commands now parses JSON API responses and has several nested branches. What do the notes recommend?
options: Add more set options so Bash catches the parsing errors
Move the logic into a scheduled cron entry with no script
Move it to a language such as Python as the logic grows
Split it into many one-line aliases in each user's profile
questions.explanation: Bash suits short, shell-oriented tasks. When parsing and logic grow, a language such as Python makes structure, error handling and testing easier.

questions.text: Which of these is a type 1 hypervisor?
options: Oracle VirtualBox
VMware ESXi
VMware Workstation
Docker Engine
questions.explanation: A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware, as ESXi and Hyper-V do. VirtualBox and VMware Workstation run on a host operating system (type 2), and Docker Engine runs containers rather than virtual machines.

questions.text: A VirtualBox guest using a NAT adapter runs a web server on port 80, but the host's browser cannot reach it. What is the usual fix while keeping NAT mode?
options: Enable a second NAT adapter on the same guest
Increase the guest's memory and CPU allocation
Add a port-forwarding rule from a host port to 80
Take a snapshot and restore it to reset the network
questions.explanation: NAT mode gives the guest outbound access, but inbound access usually needs explicit port forwarding. Alternatively, a host-only or bridged adapter can make the guest directly reachable.

questions.text: You want the host and several lab VMs to talk on a private network with no external access through that adapter. Which VirtualBox mode fits?
options: Bridged
NAT
Host-only
Internal
questions.explanation: Host-only creates a private network between the host and guests with no external access through that interface. Internal networking excludes the host too, bridged places guests on the physical network, and NAT is for outbound access.

questions.text: A VM has a host-only adapter for the lab and a second NAT adapter that was enabled during setup. What is true about its isolation?
options: It is fully isolated, because the host-only adapter takes priority
It can still reach external networks through the NAT adapter
It can be reached directly from any device on the physical LAN
It loses all connectivity, because two adapters always conflict
questions.explanation: Multiple adapters change the isolation model, and each enabled adapter adds its own reachability. The NAT adapter provides outbound access even though the host-only adapter does not. Inspect every adapter when you need isolation.

questions.text: The host disk holding a VM's files fails. The VM had several snapshots. What can you recover from the snapshots?
options: Everything, because snapshots are independent full backups
Only the most recent snapshot, which is stored in the cloud
Nothing, because snapshots depend on the VM's storage chain
All data except changes since the last scheduled snapshot
questions.explanation: A snapshot depends on the VM's own disk files and is not an independent backup. Keep important work and backups outside the disposable guest and its host storage.

questions.text: A reverse proxy and an application run on the same host. You want them to communicate without exposing a TCP listener. Which mechanism fits, and what controls who can connect?
options: A Unix-domain socket, restricted by file ownership and permissions
A UDP socket on loopback, restricted by the DNS TTL of the host
A shared memory area, restricted by the application's log level
A message broker, restricted by the order messages are acknowledged
questions.explanation: A Unix-domain socket uses a local address, often a filesystem path, so file ownership and permissions limit access. It avoids a TCP listener but still needs authorization, and container mount boundaries matter too.

questions.text: A client makes two write() calls on a TCP socket, each sending one JSON object. The server's single read() returns both objects joined together. What does this show?
options: The server's network card dropped a packet boundary marker
TCP is a byte stream, so the protocol must define framing
The client must switch to UDP to get reliable JSON delivery
Node.js merged the writes because the socket was not encrypted
questions.explanation: TCP delivers an ordered stream of bytes; one write does not guarantee one read. Define message boundaries with length prefixes, delimiters or an established protocol.

questions.text: A queue consumer charges a card and crashes before acknowledging the message. The broker redelivers it and the customer is charged twice. Which change best prevents this?
options: Acknowledge each message immediately when it is received
Run more consumer replicas so crashes affect fewer messages
Make processing idempotent, such as deduplicating by order ID
Increase the queue's maximum message size to fit the charge
questions.explanation: Brokers can deliver a message more than once, so consumers must tolerate retries. Acknowledge only after the result is safely recorded, and deduplicate repeated work. Acknowledging on receipt would lose the order if the consumer crashed.

questions.text: In the SQS lab, a consumer receives a message but crashes before calling DeleteMessage with the receipt handle. What happens to the message?
options: It is deleted, because receiving a message acknowledges it
It becomes visible again after the visibility timeout
It moves to the end of the queue with a new message ID
It is returned to the sender as a failed delivery report
questions.explanation: Receiving a message hides it only temporarily. If it is not deleted with its receipt handle before the visibility timeout ends, it becomes receivable again, so consumers must handle repeated processing.

questions.text: Two worker processes update the same shared memory region and occasionally produce corrupted totals. What is missing?
options: A TCP framing protocol between the two workers
Synchronization such as a lock around each update
A larger shared memory region for both processes
A Unix socket permission check on each update
questions.explanation: Shared memory lets processes access a common area, but they must coordinate access to avoid races and inconsistent data. A lock or other synchronization primitive makes each update atomic with respect to the other process.

questions.text: In Wireshark, which text belongs in the display filter bar to show Lab 1 traffic on port 4101?
options: tcp.port == 4101
tcp port 4101
port:4101/tcp
filter tcp 4101
questions.explanation: Display filters use field syntax such as tcp.port == 4101. tcp port 4101 is capture-filter (BPF) syntax, which belongs in the capture filter box, not the display filter.

questions.text: A team runs its application on IaaS virtual machines. Which task remains the team's responsibility?
options: Replacing failed physical disks in the data center
Patching the guest operating system on each VM
Cooling and powering the provider's server racks
Maintaining the hypervisor that hosts the VMs
questions.explanation: With IaaS the provider runs the physical infrastructure and virtualization, while you manage the guest operating system and application. PaaS shifts more of the runtime to the provider.

questions.text: A team moves its database to a managed PaaS database service. Which responsibility do they still own?
options: Installing the database engine's binaries
Replacing the underlying storage hardware
Deciding who may access the data and how
Patching the host operating system kernel
questions.explanation: PaaS manages more of the runtime or database, but you still own application behavior, data, configuration and access. The shared-responsibility split varies by service, so read it for each one.

questions.text: An application runs in two availability zones of one region. Which failure is it designed to tolerate?
options: The loss of the entire region
An outage in one zone of the region
Accidental deletion of its database
A bug in the application release
questions.explanation: Availability zones are separate locations within a region, so multiple zones limit the impact of some infrastructure failures. Surviving a regional outage needs multiple regions, and deletion or bad releases need backups and rollback.

questions.text: A subnet is named private-app, yet an instance in it is reachable from the internet. What determines whether it is actually public?
options: The subnet's name and description tags
Its routes, public addresses and firewall rules
The region where the subnet was created
The availability zone's position in the list
questions.explanation: A subnet's name does not determine reachability. Routes, public addressing, firewalls and service configuration do, so draw and verify the actual request path.

questions.text: An application needs to store user-uploaded images addressed by a key and served over HTTP. Which storage type fits best?
options: Block storage attached to a single VM
File storage shared over a network mount
Object storage that stores objects by key
A local cache in the application's memory
questions.explanation: Object storage stores objects addressed by key and is well suited to uploads and static assets. Block storage serves as a VM disk, and file storage provides shared filesystems.

questions.text: A team applies its production infrastructure template in a new account to create a staging copy. What will staging contain?
options: All production data, copied by the template automatically
New, separate resources without production's data
A read-only link to the production database
The same resources, shared between both accounts
questions.explanation: Reusing an infrastructure template creates a separate deployment; it does not copy the application's data. Use synthetic or sanitized data in non-production environments.

questions.text: A team sets a monthly budget alert for a learning account. What does the alert usually do when spending crosses the threshold?
options: Stops every resource in the account at the limit
Notifies people about spending without stopping it
Deletes the most expensive resource automatically
Lowers the account's quotas to prevent more spend
questions.explanation: Budget alerts generally report spending rather than enforcing a hard limit. Combine them with tags, ownership and regular review of idle resources, egress and logging costs.

questions.text: A nightly batch job can resume from checkpoints if it is stopped. Which compute pricing option suits it?
options: Interruptible (spot) capacity
A three-year reserved commitment
A dedicated single-tenant host
The largest on-demand instance
questions.explanation: Interruptible capacity suits workloads that tolerate termination. Reservations or commitments need a predictable demand forecast, which an occasional batch job does not provide.

questions.text: A Floci lab exercise succeeds against the local emulator. What does that prove about production AWS?
options: Production IAM policies will behave identically
Production will match the emulator's latency and timing
Little; emulator parity with production is not assured
The same code is certified for compliance audits
questions.explanation: Emulators are useful for learning AWS-style APIs, but they do not establish production service or IAM parity, timing or eventual-consistency behavior.

questions.text: terraform validate succeeds. What has it confirmed?
options: The target account has permission to create the resources
The cloud provider has capacity for every requested resource
The configuration is internally consistent and well-formed
The plan will cost less than the project's monthly budget
questions.explanation: Validation checks configuration consistency, not service availability, access rights, cost or every provider constraint. Those only surface during planning or applying against the real provider.

questions.text: A reviewer approved the output of terraform plan -out=tfplan. What happens when you run terraform apply tfplan?
options: Terraform recalculates a fresh plan and asks for approval again
Terraform executes the saved plan without another approval prompt
Terraform applies only the resources marked for creation
Terraform discards the saved plan if any file was formatted
questions.explanation: Applying a saved plan runs exactly those proposed actions without an interactive prompt, so review belongs before this step. Confirm the account, environment and workspace before planning.

questions.text:
A plan output includes the following line for a database. What should the reviewer understand?

  # aws_db_instance.main must be replaced
-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
      ~ identifier = "orders-db" -> "orders-db-v2" # forces replacement
options: Terraform will update the database in place with no downtime
Terraform will skip the resource because nothing has changed
Terraform will destroy and recreate the database instance
Terraform will only refresh the database's state attributes
questions.explanation: -/+ marks a replacement: the existing object is destroyed and a new one created (or the reverse with create_before_destroy). For persistent data, treat replacement and deletion actions very differently from updates.

questions.text: A colleague's terraform apply is running, and your plan fails because the state is locked. What should you do?
options: Force-unlock the state so your plan can run immediately
Copy the state file locally and plan against that copy
Wait for their operation to finish, then plan again
Disable locking in the backend configuration permanently
questions.explanation: Locking prevents concurrent writers from corrupting state. Coordinate writers and do not disable or bypass locking to get around another operation.

questions.text: A Terraform output is marked sensitive = true. Where can the value still be found?
options: Nowhere, because Terraform encrypts it before storing
Only in the provider's API, never on disk
In the state file, which must itself be protected
Only in .terraform.lock.hcl, which must stay private
questions.explanation: sensitive hides values from normal display but does not remove them from state or saved plans. Use a remote backend with access controls and encryption, and keep state and plans out of Git.

questions.text: Which Terraform file should be committed to version control?
options: terraform.tfstate
The saved tfplan file
.terraform.lock.hcl
A secrets.tfvars file
questions.explanation: Commit configuration and the provider dependency lockfile, .terraform.lock.hcl, so everyone uses the same provider versions. State, saved plans and secret variable files can contain sensitive values and stay out of Git.

questions.text: Someone runs terraform state rm aws_s3_bucket.logs. What happens to the real bucket?
options: It is deleted on the next terraform apply
It keeps existing, but Terraform no longer manages it
It is moved to a new address in the same state
It is emptied of all objects but kept as a managed resource
questions.explanation: Removing an object from state stops Terraform managing it; it does not delete the remote object. If the configuration still declares the bucket, a later plan would propose creating a new one.

questions.text:
You rename a resource block from aws_instance.web to aws_instance.app without changing its settings. The plan wants to destroy and recreate it. What is the supported fix?

resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  ami           = var.ami_id
  instance_type = "t3.small"
}
options: Edit the state JSON by hand to change the address
Add a moved block from the old to the new address
Run terraform apply and accept the replacement
Delete .terraform.lock.hcl and run init again
questions.explanation: Use supported move mechanisms, such as a moved block or terraform state mv, when refactoring addresses. Editing state JSON directly is an exceptional repair task that needs a backup and recovery plan.

questions.text: A team uses Terraform CLI workspaces named dev and prod in the same backend. What do the workspaces provide by themselves?
options: Separate state instances, but no access-control boundary
Separate cloud accounts with distinct credential policies
Automatic approval gates before any prod apply
Encrypted state for prod but plain text for dev
questions.explanation: CLI workspaces separate state instances but do not create an access-control boundary. Give environments separate state and appropriate credential boundaries, such as different backends and roles.

questions.text: A team hopes to apply its AWS network module unchanged to another cloud provider because both are managed with Terraform. Why will this fail?
options: Terraform cannot manage more than one provider per project
Resources are provider-specific even with shared syntax
Network resources cannot be placed in modules
Modules can only be used once per Terraform version
questions.explanation: Terraform can use many providers, but each provider's resources and arguments differ. A different cloud needs its own resource definitions, even if the module's inputs and structure look similar.

questions.text: An engineer changed a firewall rule in the console during an incident to stop an attack. The next plan proposes reverting it. What should happen?
options: Apply the plan immediately so the configuration is authoritative
Delete the rule from state so Terraform stops tracking it
Review the drift and update the configuration to keep the fix
Destroy and recreate the firewall to clear the difference
questions.explanation: Drift is a change outside the declared configuration and should be reviewed before accepting or correcting it. Blindly applying an old configuration can undo a necessary repair; reconcile the emergency change into the source of truth.

questions.text: A team must create a VM, then manage the packages, users and service configuration inside it. Which split of tools fits?
options: Ansible creates the VM; Terraform manages the packages
Terraform provisions the VM; Ansible configures the OS
Packer manages running VMs; Argo CD installs packages
Docker creates the VM; Kubernetes manages its users
questions.explanation: Terraform provisions infrastructure through provider APIs, but it does not generally enforce files and packages inside a VM. Configuration management such as Ansible handles the operating system, or Packer can bake those settings into an image.

questions.text: A team wants every new VM to start from a patched base image with their agent preinstalled. Which tool is designed for building that image?
options: Packer
Argo CD
Compose
Flux
questions.explanation: Packer builds machine images, often running scripts or Ansible during the build; Terraform can then deploy instances from the image. Argo CD and Flux reconcile cluster state, and Compose runs groups of containers.

questions.text: Terraform sets an instance group's size to 3, and an autoscaler raises it to 6 during peaks. Every plan proposes shrinking it back. What is the underlying problem?
options: The autoscaler should be removed so Terraform is in control
Two controllers own the same setting without clear division
Terraform's state is corrupted and should be deleted
The instance group must be recreated on each apply
questions.explanation: Do not let two controllers continually overwrite the same setting. Define ownership, for example letting the autoscaler own the count while Terraform ignores changes to it, and document which differences are expected.

questions.text: A small team runs one web app and a managed database, deployed by a repeatable script to a single VM. Someone proposes adopting Kubernetes. What should decide this?
options: Kubernetes is required for any containerized application
Kubernetes removes the need to manage node operating systems
Whether scheduling, scaling and rollout needs justify its cost
Whether the cloud provider offers a free Kubernetes control plane
questions.explanation: Kubernetes becomes useful when scheduling, scaling, isolation and rollout requirements justify operating the platform. Compare the cost of running and learning a tool with the manual work it removes.

questions.text: Do Kubernetes nodes need Docker Engine installed to run container images?
options: Yes, Kubernetes can only start containers through Docker Engine
No, nodes can use any compatible container runtime
Yes, but only for images built with a Dockerfile
No, Kubernetes runs images as virtual machines instead
questions.explanation: Kubernetes uses compatible container runtimes, such as containerd or CRI-O, through its runtime interface. Images built with Docker follow the OCI format and run without Docker Engine on the nodes.

questions.text: How does a container differ from a virtual machine?
options: A container has its own guest kernel; a VM shares the host's
Containers share a kernel; a VM runs its own guest kernel
A container always runs exactly one process; a VM runs many
Containers need a type 1 hypervisor; VMs need a type 2 one
questions.explanation: A container is an isolated process environment that shares the kernel of its runtime environment, while a VM has its own guest kernel on virtual hardware. Containers are not restricted to exactly one process.

questions.text: A PostgreSQL container stores data in its writable layer. The container is removed and recreated from the same image. What happens to the data?
options: It is restored from the image's previous layer automatically
It is lost, because the writable layer goes with the container
It is preserved, because the image tag has not changed
It is moved into a volume that Docker creates on removal
questions.explanation: Files in a container's writable layer disappear when the container is removed. Use a volume or an external service for persistent data, and still back it up, since a volume alone is not a backup.

questions.text: A Dockerfile copies credentials.json in one step and deletes it in a later RUN step. Is the secret gone from the image?
options: Yes, deleting the file removes it from every layer
No, it remains in the earlier layer of the image
Yes, as long as the image is pushed with a new tag
No, but only if the image runs as the root user
questions.explanation: Each instruction creates a layer, and a later deletion only hides the file in the final filesystem. Keep secrets out of image layers and deliver them at runtime; multi-stage builds help keep build-time files out of the final image.

questions.text: Why use a multi-stage Docker build for a compiled application?
options: The final image can omit compilers and build tools
The image can run on hosts that lack a container runtime
Each stage receives its own kernel at runtime
The build no longer needs a pinned base image
questions.explanation: A multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the needed outputs into a small runtime stage, reducing image size and attack surface. It does not change how containers use the host kernel.

questions.text: During a rolling update, old containers are killed abruptly and users see failed requests. Which application change helps most?
options: Writing logs to a file inside the container
Running the application as the root user
Handling SIGTERM to finish in-flight requests
Using the latest tag for every release
questions.explanation: Orchestrators send a termination signal before killing a container. Handling it to stop accepting new work and finish or abandon in-flight work cleanly, within the grace period, avoids dropped requests.

questions.text: A web application with a built-in scheduler is scaled from one to three replicas. What new problem is likely?
options: The scheduler stops running because replicas share a port
Each replica runs the scheduled task, so it runs three times
The load balancer routes all requests to a single replica
The image becomes three times larger to support replicas
questions.explanation: Scaling web replicas should not accidentally duplicate a scheduler. Separate request handling from scheduled work and workers when their lifecycles differ, and design jobs to tolerate retries.

questions.text: A Pod is running but still warming its cache, and it should not receive traffic yet. Which probe controls this?
options: Readiness probe
Liveness probe
Restart policy
Resource limit
questions.explanation: A readiness probe decides whether a workload should receive traffic. A liveness probe can trigger a restart, and a startup probe gives slow-starting applications time to initialize before other probes apply.

questions.text: A liveness probe calls an endpoint that checks the database. During a database outage, every Pod restarts repeatedly. What was the mistake?
options: The readiness probe should have been removed entirely
Liveness depended on an external dependency's health
The Pods needed more replicas to survive the outage
The database should have used a liveness probe too
questions.explanation: A liveness failure restarts the container, and restarting does not fix the database. A poorly chosen liveness probe turns a dependency outage into repeated restarts; keep liveness about the process itself.

questions.text: In Kubernetes, which object gives a stable network address for a changing set of Pods managed by a Deployment?
options: A ConfigMap
A CronJob
A Service
A PersistentVolume
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages replicated Pods and rollouts, while a Service selects Pods by label and provides a stable name and address in front of them. ConfigMaps hold configuration, and PersistentVolumes provide storage.

questions.text: You run docker compose config to share the resolved configuration with a vendor. What should you check first?
options: Whether the output includes every image's full layers
Whether it shows secret values from environment files
Whether it will restart the running services
Whether it deletes volumes listed in the file
questions.explanation: docker compose config prints the resolved configuration, which may include values interpolated from environment variables or .env files. Handle it as potentially sensitive before sharing. It does not start, stop or delete anything.

questions.text: A checkout request is slow, and it passes through a gateway, an order service, a payment service and a database. Which signal best shows where the time was spent?
options: A metric of total requests per minute
A distributed trace of that request
A log line from the gateway's startup
A dashboard of average CPU per host
questions.explanation: Traces connect operations across a request's path through several components, showing the duration of each span. Metrics summarize measurements over time, and logs describe individual events with context.

questions.text: Average latency for an API is 120 ms, yet users complain that some requests take several seconds. Which measurement reveals the problem?
options: The mean latency over a longer window
The total number of requests per day
A high percentile such as p99 latency
The minimum latency seen per instance
questions.explanation: Percentiles reveal slow tails that an average can hide. Also separate successful and failed request latency, since fast errors can make an average look healthy.

questions.text: A developer adds a user_id label to a request-count metric, and the metrics backend's memory use explodes. Why?
options: Each distinct user ID creates a new time series
Labels are stored as logs instead of metrics
Prometheus cannot store numeric label values
The metric was converted into a distributed trace
questions.explanation: Every unique label combination is a separate time series, so unbounded values such as user IDs or arbitrary paths create too many. Keep labels bounded and put per-request detail in restricted logs or traces.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes an SLI from an SLO?
options: An SLI is a contract penalty; an SLO is a dashboard panel
An SLI measures a result; an SLO sets its target and window
An SLI is set by customers; an SLO is set by the provider
An SLI covers latency only; an SLO covers availability only
questions.explanation: A service-level indicator measures a result, such as the fraction of valid requests that succeed. A service-level objective sets the target for that indicator over a time window, such as 99.9% over 30 days.

questions.text: A service has a 99.9% request-success SLO over 30 days and receives 2,000,000 eligible requests in that window. How many failed requests does the error budget allow?
questions.explanation: The error budget is the allowed failure fraction, 0.1%, of eligible requests: $0.001 \times 2{,}000{,}000 = 2{,}000$. Define which requests are eligible and what counts as success before calculating.

questions.text: Which situation justifies paging an on-call engineer immediately?
options: A disk will reach 80% capacity in about three weeks
Checkout failures are rising and customers are affected
A nightly report job ran five minutes slower than usual
A dependency released a new minor version upstream
questions.explanation: Page someone when timely action is needed for a significant service impact. Slower capacity and maintenance issues belong in tickets or scheduled review.

questions.text: Errors spike right after a deployment. The cause is not yet understood. What is the best first mitigation?
options: Stop or roll back the rollout using a known procedure
Debug in production until the root cause is confirmed
Change several configuration settings at the same time
Delete the logs from the period to reduce the noise
questions.explanation: Mitigate with a known action, such as stopping a rollout, before completing the investigation. Preserve evidence and avoid changing several unrelated things at once, then verify recovery with user-facing signals.

questions.text: A user signs in successfully with a valid token, then tries to delete another team's project. Which control should stop the request?
options: Authentication, since the token proves who the user is
Authorization, which decides what that identity may do
TLS, which encrypts the request on its way to the server
Network reachability, since the user reached the endpoint
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization determines what it may do. Network reachability and encryption are not proof that a request should be accepted.

questions.text: A cloud role has narrow permissions, but its trust policy allows any principal in the account to assume it. Why is this a problem?
options: Trust policies only matter for roles used by humans
The trust policy decides who may assume the role at all
Narrow permissions are ignored when trust is broad
A role cannot have both permissions and a trust policy
questions.explanation: Restrict role trust as well as permissions. The permissions say what the role can do, while the trust policy says who may assume it, so broad trust lets unintended identities gain those permissions.

questions.text: An API token was pasted into a public chat channel. What is the correct first action?
options: Delete the message and assume the token is now safe
Revoke or replace the token, then investigate its use
Rewrite Git history to remove any copies of the token
Ask channel members to confirm they did not copy it
questions.explanation: Removing a secret from its current location does not invalidate copies in logs, caches or history. Revoke or replace it first, investigate how it was used, and plan any cleanup afterwards.

questions.text: A team plans to rotate a database password every 90 days. What should they test before relying on rotation?
options: That the new password is longer than the old one
That dependent services reload it without an outage
That the password appears in the deployment logs
That the old password stays valid after rotation
questions.explanation: Document who owns each secret, how applications reload it and how to replace it, then test rotation with the dependent services so a credential change does not cause an outage.

questions.text: Which test verifies that an access boundary actually works?
options: Confirm the restricted role can perform its normal tasks
Confirm the restricted role is denied an action outside it
Confirm the role's policy document is valid JSON
Confirm the role appears in the account's role list
questions.explanation: A boundary is proven by a denied request, not by successful normal work. Also test that expired credentials stop working and that important administrative actions are logged.

questions.text: A team moved PostgreSQL from port 5432 to 6543 and renamed the admin user, calling the database "secured." What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Port 6543 is reserved and will conflict with other services
PostgreSQL only accepts TLS connections on port 5432
It does not replace network controls and authentication
Renaming the admin user disables password authentication
questions.explanation: Changing a default port or username does not replace network controls and authenticated connections. Keep the database reachable only by clients that need it, use TLS with verification and give each client a separate least-privilege identity.

questions.text: A query has become slow as a table grew. Someone proposes upgrading to a larger database instance. What should come first?
options: Double the connection pool size for the application
Review the slow query log and the query's execution plan
Add an index on every single column that the table contains
Restart the database to clear its memory caches
questions.explanation: Review slow queries and execution plans before assuming the answer is a larger instance. A missing index or an unbounded query is a common cause, and indexes also add storage and write cost, so add them deliberately.

questions.text: You need to rename the column fullname to display_name while old and new application versions run together. Which sequence follows expand-and-contract?
options: Rename fullname in one migration, then deploy code using the new name
Drop fullname, add display_name, then redeploy every version at once
Add display_name, write both, backfill, switch reads, drop fullname
Deploy code reading only display_name, then add and backfill the column
questions.explanation: Expand-and-contract adds a compatible field, deploys code that can use it, backfills safely, switches reads, and removes the old field only after older versions no longer depend on it. A direct rename breaks the version still running.

questions.text: A migration converts prices from cents to rounded whole currency units. The team says, "we can always run the down migration." Why is that unsafe?
options: Down migrations can only run on the primary replica
The transformation loses data, so it may not reverse
Down migrations are always applied automatically
Rounding is reversed when the column type changes
questions.explanation: Not every migration has a lossless inverse. Dropping a column or transforming data can be irreversible, so write a recovery strategy for risky changes, which may mean fixing forward or restoring data.

questions.text: A database has a synchronous replica in another zone. Someone runs DELETE FROM orders; by mistake. What does the replica provide?
options: A clean copy of the orders from before the delete
Nothing for this case, since it copies the delete too
An automatic rollback of the transaction on the primary
A frozen snapshot of the table taken at the last hour
questions.explanation: Replication across failure domains reduces downtime but also copies accidental deletion or corruption. High availability and backups solve different problems, so the orders must come from a protected backup or point-in-time recovery.

questions.text: A shop can lose at most 15 minutes of orders and must be serving again within one hour after a failure. How are these targets expressed?
options: RPO of 15 minutes, RTO of one hour
RTO of 15 minutes, RPO of one hour
SLO of 15 minutes, SLI of one hour
RPO and RTO both set at one hour
questions.explanation: The recovery point objective is the acceptable data loss measured in time, and the recovery time objective is how long restoration may take. Both must be met: recent enough data and a restore that fits within an hour.

questions.text: A service has an RPO of 15 minutes, but its only database backup runs nightly at 02:00. What is the gap?
options: The RTO is too short for a nightly backup to restore
Up to about 24 hours of data could be lost
Nightly backups always meet any RPO under one day
The backup must also be copied to a second region
questions.explanation: With only nightly backups, a failure just before the next backup loses almost a day of writes, far beyond 15 minutes. Meeting the RPO needs more frequent recovery points, such as continuous log archiving or point-in-time recovery.

questions.text: A team keeps its production data plus two backup copies, on two different storage types, with one copy off-site. Which rule does this follow?
options: The 2-1-0 rule
The 3-2-1 rule
The 1-1-1 rule
The 3-3-3 rule
questions.explanation: The 3-2-1 rule means three copies of data, on two different media or storage types, with one copy off-site. It keeps copies separate from the original failure domain; many teams also add an immutable or offline copy.

questions.text: The backup job has reported success every night for a year. What actually proves the backups are usable?
options: The job's exit code and the size of each backup file
Restoring one into a separate environment and testing it
Confirming the backup bucket has versioning enabled
Checking that backups are encrypted with a current key
questions.explanation: A backup is useful only if the service can be restored from it within the required time and data loss. Restore into a separate environment, validate data and workflows, and measure the elapsed time and data gap.

questions.text: An engineer backs up a busy database by copying its data directory with cp -r while the server runs. What is the risk?
options: The copy will be too large to compress efficiently
The copied files may not form a consistent database
The database will lose its data directory after copying
The copy will include the database's TLS private key
questions.explanation: A filesystem copy of live database files may capture them mid-write and not be a usable backup. Use the engine's backup tools or a consistent snapshot mechanism, and verify by restoring.

questions.text: During a restore drill of production data into a test environment, what should be disabled?
options: Database authentication for the restored copy
Destructive or externally visible background jobs
Monitoring and logs for the test environment
The backup schedule for the production database
questions.explanation: A restored copy can contain scheduled jobs that send emails, charge cards or delete data. Keep destructive or externally visible jobs disabled during drills, and coordinate writes and traffic during a real cutover.

questions.text: On Amazon RDS, you run point-in-time recovery to 09:58, just before a bad deletion at 10:00. What happens?
options: The existing instance is rewound in place to 09:58
A new instance is created with data as of 09:58
Only the deleted rows are copied back into the table
The application is reconnected to the restored data
questions.explanation: RDS point-in-time recovery creates a new DB instance. Validating it, reconnecting the application and switching traffic are extra steps, and writes after 09:58 may need reconciliation.

questions.text: A small company's servers were configured by hand over several years. What should happen before broad configuration changes?
options: Move every server into Kubernetes in one project
Inventory the servers and confirm a restore works
Reinstall every server from the same new OS image
Write an Ansible role covering every possible setting
questions.explanation: Record each server's purpose, owner, services, dependencies, jobs and data locations, and back up and test a restore before changing things. Then automate one low-risk task and expand gradually.

questions.text: An Ansible playbook is run a second time against the same host with no changes in between. What indicates its tasks are idempotent?
options: Every task reports changed on both runs
The second run reports no new changes
The second run is skipped by Ansible automatically
The playbook fails if the host is already configured
questions.explanation: An idempotent task converges on the desired state and does not report a change when it is already there. Prefer modules that describe the desired state over shell commands that run unconditionally.

questions.text: A playbook is run with --check --diff and shows the expected changes. What does this not guarantee?
options: That the application works after the change
That the playbook syntax could be parsed
That the inventory targets could be reached
That Ansible computed a predicted result
questions.explanation: Check and diff modes help review changes, but support depends on the module, and neither proves the application will work. Diffs may also expose secrets, so review where the output goes.

questions.text: A playbook changes the SSH configuration on 40 servers. Which rollout is safest?
options: Apply it to all 40 servers at once so they stay consistent
Apply it by hand on each server, then update the playbook
Keep a recovery path, change a small batch, verify, expand
Disable password access everywhere before testing the keys
questions.explanation: Roll out to a small batch, verify health and stop on failure. When changing SSH, firewall or admin settings, keep a recovery access method so a failed rollout does not lock everyone out.

questions.text: A team moves a scheduled cleanup into a Kubernetes CronJob with overlapping runs forbidden. Is the cleanup now guaranteed to run exactly once per schedule?
options: Yes, forbidding overlap guarantees exactly-once runs
No, so the job should still be idempotent or locked
Yes, as long as the CronJob has only one replica
No, CronJobs always run once per node in the cluster
questions.explanation: A CronJob can limit overlapping jobs from the same CronJob, but scheduling is not an exactly-once guarantee; runs can be missed or repeated. Use idempotency or locking where duplicate work would be harmful.

questions.text: A monolith runs behind a load balancer with three replicas, all using one database on a single unprotected host. How available is the service?
options: Highly available, because there are three replicas
Highly available, because the load balancer reroutes
Limited by the database, a single point of failure
Limited by the monolith, which cannot be replicated
questions.explanation: Multiple replicas help only when shared dependencies support them. A load balancer cannot make a single unprotected database highly available. A monolith can be packaged and replicated reliably.

questions.text: A team wants to rebuild a model from six months ago. They have the training code commit. What else must have been recorded?
options: Only the Python interpreter version used for serving
The dataset version, features, parameters and seeds
Only the evaluation score reported to stakeholders
The name of the engineer who trained the model
questions.explanation: Model behavior depends on code, data, features and training configuration. Record the dataset version or immutable reference, feature transformations, parameters, dependencies, random seeds and evaluation results with the artifact.

questions.text: A model scores well offline, but in production its predictions are poor because the serving code computes a feature differently from the training pipeline. What is this called?
options: Concept drift
Data leakage
Training-serving skew
Label shift
questions.explanation: Training-serving skew is a difference between feature processing during training and inference. Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, and data leakage is test information contaminating training.

questions.text: A fraud model's input distribution is unchanged, but fraudsters have adopted new tactics, so the same inputs now indicate different outcomes. What is this?
options: Data drift
Concept drift
Training-serving skew
A schema change
questions.explanation: Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the intended outcome. Data drift is a change in the input distribution, which can occur without predictions getting worse.

questions.text: A model's overall accuracy is 94%, but complaints come from one customer region. What practice would have exposed this before release?
options: Reporting only the overall accuracy to more decimal places
Recording evaluation slices that matter to the application
Training on the test set to increase overall accuracy
Retraining automatically every night on all new data
questions.explanation: An average score can hide poor performance for a particular group or scenario. Record evaluation slices that matter, and keep training, validation and test data separate to avoid leakage.

questions.text: A team wants to see how a candidate model behaves on real production inputs without affecting any user decisions. Which approach fits?
options: Shadow traffic sent to the candidate model
A controlled experiment that serves both models
Automatic promotion after nightly retraining
Replacing the current model during low traffic
questions.explanation: Shadow traffic reveals serving behavior without affecting user decisions, while a controlled experiment measures product impact by exposing users to the candidate. Both need care around load and privacy.

questions.text: Database backups are written to Cloud Storage daily, kept for at least two months, and restored about once a month for testing. Which storage class is the most cost-effective?
options: Standard
Nearline
Coldline
Archive
questions.explanation: Nearline suits data read about once a month and has a 30-day minimum storage duration. Coldline and Archive store data more cheaply but charge more for each retrieval and have longer minimum durations.

questions.text: Records must be retained for ten years for regulatory reasons and will almost never be read. Which storage class should you choose?
options: Nearline
Coldline
Archive
Standard
questions.explanation: Archive has the lowest storage price, a 365-day minimum storage duration and the highest retrieval cost, which fits data accessed less than once a year. All classes keep millisecond access latency.

questions.text: A bucket holds millions of objects with unpredictable and changing access patterns, and the team does not want to write or maintain storage class transition rules. What should you do?
options: Keep all objects in Standard to avoid retrieval charges
Enable Autoclass on the bucket
Write a nightly job that rewrites cold objects to Archive
Create a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Coldline after 30 days
